audio_segments.text: Hello!
Welcome to this course IC Design Process, a beginner's overview to VLSI technology.
This course is presented by System Veralog Academy.
It is an online platform to learn System Veralog hardware description language for both design and verification coding.
Visit us at SystemVeralogAcademy.com for in-depth system-verilog trainings in all levels of expertness, beginner, intermediate or advanced.
This is a beginner-level course.
When anybody start learning a hardware description language such as System Veralog or VHDL, the most common problem they could face is,
in connecting what they write in their program to the actual circuit that get produced in the silicon.
This is a course designed to simplify this problem.
By connecting together the pieces of information scattered throughout RTL design, functional verification, synthesis, physical design, and manufacturing in VLSI technology.
This is not teaching any specific hardware description language or anything related to coding in an HDL.
Course Overview
As this course is teaching more theory than coding practices, it is designed to be a short one and gives only the overview of every process.
The first session explains a short history of ICs.
Second session refreshes few fundamentals of digital circuits.
Third session describes the idea of hardware description language.
Fourth session gives the overview of every steps involved in the design process of an IC.
It is broadly classified as front end and back end design processes.
Fifth session briefs the IC manufacturing process and the final session summaries the course.
History of ICs
An integrated circuit or IC is a device with a large number of electronic circuits built into a tiny plate of semiconductor material, which will be usually silicon.
An SOC or system on chip is an IC with all components of a complete electronic system built into a single silicon plate, or simply an SOC is a device with multiple ICs built in a single chip.
Even though the actual silicon in an IC is a tiny metal piece, they could be built with up to several billions of transistors and other electronic components in it.
As you know, there are two categories of electronic circuits, analog and digital.
In the same manner, ICs can also be analog or digital based on the number of operational voltage levels in them.
Designed process of analog and digital ICs are not very similar, but the manufacturing process for both of them are almost similar.
Usually, HDLs are used to design digital ICs, and this course is explaining the process on the grounds of a digital IC.
Every digital circuit is made of switches that turn on and turn off the voltage.
Before the invention of BJT, the bipolar junction transistor, circuits were using vacuum tubes as these digital switches.
You can imagine how bulky was even a simple laboratory circuit that used vacuum tubes instead of transistors.
With the invention of transistors in 1947 at Bell Laboratories, vacuum tubes were replaced by the small silicon devices, but still the whole circuit was made of discrete transistors.

Eventually, the idea came up that proposed to build all transistors and other components in a whole electronic circuit into a single silicon piece, instead of manufacturing them separately and assembling.
This was nothing but what we call as an integrated circuit, and from there, IC technology evolution started and made it possible to build up to billions of components into a single wafer.
VLSI

The first integrated circuits build only a few devices in them. Perhaps as many as 10 diodes, transistors, resistors, and capacitors, making it possible to fabricate one or two logic gates on a single IC.
This number started to increase slowly and got up to billion in 2008.
Based on the number of transistors made into a single chip, the manufacturing technologies were known by different names in the industry, like SSI or LSI.
Early in the 1960s, hundreds of transistors were built into a single chip, and technology was commonly known as SSI or small-scale integration.
It went up to thousands of transistors in late 1960s, which was known as medium-scale integration, MSI.
In 70s, it increased to tens of thousands of transistors, and the technology was known as large-scale integration or LSI.
Eventually, the number of transistors in a single chip increased to hundreds of thousands of transistors in 1980s, millions in late 90s, and to billions in 2008.
Nowadays, irrespective of the number of transistors in the chip, all IC manufacturing technologies are called by the same name, VLSI or very large-scale integration.
